reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours of Soft Tissue and Bone
clinicalPearls: One of the commoner sarcomas of elderly patients, arising typically in the dermal and subcutaneous soft tissue of the limbs and limb girdles
Characteristically shows a fibroblastic tumour with variably myxoid stroma, curvilinear vessels, and a spectrum of grades from low to high
Notorious for an infiltrative growth pattern with finger-like extensions along fascial planes that extend well beyond the apparent mass, driving a high local recurrence rate
Presents as a slowly enlarging, often painless subcutaneous mass, which may be mistaken for a benign lesion, especially when low grade
MRI often reveals infiltrative tails of tumour along fascia (the tail sign), helping to plan resection margins
Genomically complex with highly aberrant karyotypes rather than a defining recurrent fusion
Wide surgical excision with generous margins is essential, frequently combined with radiotherapy to reduce local recurrence, with chemotherapy reserved for selected high-grade cases
Repeated local recurrences may be accompanied by progression to higher grade and increasing metastatic potential
reference.pathophysiology: Myxofibrosarcoma is a malignant fibroblastic tumour with a characteristically myxoid stroma and prominent curvilinear vasculature. It is genomically complex, showing marked chromosomal instability and copy-number changes rather than a single defining genetic event, which places it among the karyotypically complex sarcomas. Its striking tendency to infiltrate diffusely along fascial and subcutaneous planes, often extending microscopically far beyond the palpable or radiologically evident mass, underlies its high propensity for local recurrence. With repeated recurrence, tumours often increase in grade and cellularity, acquiring greater metastatic potential, most commonly to the lungs.
additionalDifferentials: Nodular fasciitis and other benign myxoid lesions
Superficial soft-tissue benign masses (e.g. lipoma, ganglion)
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the primary site to identify infiltrative fascial tails and define true extent
Chest CT for pulmonary metastases in higher-grade disease
Whole-body functional imaging for staging where indicated
Core biopsy with careful tract planning
Immunohistochemistry to exclude specific differentiation and other myxoid tumours
Molecular testing to exclude entities such as myxoid liposarcoma and low-grade fibromyxoid sarcoma
redFlags: An enlarging subcutaneous mass in an elderly patient, particularly if previously excised locally
Repeated local recurrence at a prior excision site
Increasing size, firmness, or pain suggesting progression to higher grade
New respiratory symptoms indicating pulmonary metastases
Extensive infiltrative disease on imaging beyond the palpable mass
reference.prognosis: Prognosis relates chiefly to grade and adequacy of excision; low-grade tumours rarely metastasise but recur locally, whereas high-grade tumours carry a significant metastatic risk, and repeated recurrence with grade progression worsens the outlook.
pitfalls: Underestimating tumour extent because infiltrative tails reach well beyond the visible mass, leading to inadequate margins
Mistaking a low-grade tumour for a benign myxoid lesion and performing marginal excision
Confusing myxofibrosarcoma with myxoid liposarcoma or low-grade fibromyxoid sarcoma without molecular testing
Neglecting adjuvant radiotherapy where indicated, contributing to local recurrence
Failing to reassess grade at recurrence, missing progression to higher-grade disease
references: WHO Classification of Tumours of Soft Tissue and Bone
Enzinger and Weiss's Soft Tissue Tumors
management: Refer any suspected or confirmed myxofibrosarcoma to a multidisciplinary soft tissue sarcoma team (surgical oncology, radiation oncology, medical oncology, pathology) before definitive treatment
Wide local excision with clear margins is the definitive treatment for localized, resectable disease of any grade
Plan resection assuming disease extends beyond what imaging or palpation suggests, given the tumor's tendency to infiltrate along fascial planes
Consider perioperative radiotherapy (neoadjuvant or adjuvant) for high-grade, large, deep, or marginally resectable tumors to reduce local recurrence

Consider cytotoxic systemic therapy, typically an anthracycline based regimen alone or with an alkylating agent such as ifosfamide, in selected high risk locally advanced cases as part of a multidisciplinary plan
For isolated resectable pulmonary metastases, consider metastasectomy; for disseminated metastatic disease, systemic therapy plus supportive and palliative care are the mainstay
At any local recurrence, re-stage and repeat pathological grading rather than assuming the original grade still applies, since recurrences can be higher grade
Structured surveillance should include regular clinical exam of the surgical site plus periodic local imaging, and chest imaging directed by the known pattern of lung, bone, and lymph node spread
Refer promptly for re-evaluation at any local recurrence given the risk of grade progression and rising metastatic potential
Refer patients with high grade, large, or metastatic disease, or those who may be candidates for investigational therapy, to a center with access to sarcoma clinical trials
mTOR pathway inhibition and Skp2/neddylation inhibition are investigational strategies under early phase and preclinical study, not standard of care, and should only be pursued in a trial setting
